item.title: Hilton Dips, JetBlue Rallies | Stock Movers
item.description:
Today's biggest winners and losers in the stock market. On this episode of Stock Movers: - Hilton Worldwide (HLT) is falling after the hotel operator gave a forecast for adjusted earnings per share for the fourth quarter that fell short of the average analyst estimate. - JetBlue (JBLU) shares are rallying after the carrier reiterated its expectation to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share and positive free cash flow in 2028. The shares closed Monday at a record low as the airline grapples with cash burn and elevated oil prices. - Boeing (BA) shares are on the move after posted a quarterly loss after higher costs affected its commercial-jet business. The company's total revenue grew about 4% to $24.19 billion, driven in part by stronger sales from its defense, space and security business. Boeing generated cash despite the loss, and its 737 program is progressing toward stabilized production at 47 jets a month. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: From Blackouts to Surplus: How Eskom Turned South Africa’s Power Around
item.description:
After enduring years of crippling power cuts, South Africa’s state utility Eskom has swung to an operational surplus, maintaining 3 to 5 gigawatts of excess generation capacity, according to CEO Dan Marokane. Yet across Johannesburg, localized outages persist as the city works to strengthen its finances and manage its power network. Speaking to Bloomberg’s Jennifer Zabasajja on Next Africa, Marokane discusses the city’s progress on settling overdue electricity bills and plans to ring-fence electricity revenue. He also outlines how Eskom’s recovery is enabling cross-border exports to neighboring southern African states, and explains why reliable electricity is central to rebuilding Johannesburg’s economy. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods
item.description:
It's obvious that things are getting more expensive, and there are plenty of reasons behind the surge in prices — whether it's wars or inflation or companies padding their profit margins. But with the release of AI agents like Meta's Muse, tech companies are promising consumers that agents will start saving them tons of money by finding the best deals. According to today's guest, Lindsay Owens, the history of price gouging does not bode well for claims that things might get cheaper because of new technology, and research conducted by her think tank Groundwork Collaborative shows that a number of consumer facing agents end up serving customers more expensive items after learning more about their financial situation. Her new book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet gets into the history of how companies got away with charging more for their goods, through means like data collection and surveillance. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature
item.description:
In 1776, the field of economics was born with the publication of Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations. Among the book's earliest readers was a Regency-era novelist named Maria Edgeworth. In her time, Edgeworth was one of the most famous literary figures in England, and she smuggled into her stories economic concepts and debates around rent seeking, the idea of productive labor, and so on. These works were enormously influential and they helped expose a generation to practical applications of Smith's theories. Jeanna Smialek, a veteran Fed reporter and the Brussels bureau chief at The New York Times, thinks Edgeworth's name needs to be placed back in the pantheon of economic history. Today, we discuss Edgeworth's friendly debates with the likes of Thomas Malthus and David Ricardo, how the Irish potato famine reshaped economic thought, and how Edgeworth used the novel form to educate the masses on the value of economics. (Source: Bloomberg)

Gower said mine supply is expected to fall this year, with further risks next year from project recoveries and potential strikes in Chile and the U.S. Other possible supports include continued tariff-related stockpiling, stronger AI demand and Chinese stimulus. But China’s end-use indicators are mixed, and weakness in construction and property remains a concern. The discussion also noted that copper’s recent gains are struggling to extend. item.author: Olivia Solon, Tom Mackenzie and Christina Kyriasoglou

item.title: Bhaskar Sunkara Thinks the Market Has a Place Under Socialism
item.description:
In September, Gallup released a poll that showed that 43% percent of Americans viewed socialism positively, the highest approval since Gallup began the poll back in 2010. Since Zohran Mamdani won the NYC mayoral election, the left has made a number of gains across national politics. As a longtime DSA member and veteran of leftist media, Bhaskar Sunkara is one of socialism's leading advocates, and he's spent much of his career charting what a socialist economy in America might look like. Unlike some other leftists, he believes the market has a place. In fact, he thinks markets and entrepreneurs are an objective good in society. He proposes a vision of so-called "market socialism" in his recent co-authored book The Blueprint, and he lays out this system for us in today's episode. We talk about how many features of capitalism — from small businesses to monetary policy — might be remade under socialist principles. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Berlin, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, global stocks fell after a mixed start to US tech earnings failed to calm nerves around the AI trade. Meta doubled down on its investment plans, boosting its capital spending forecast for the year. Oil advanced after deadly Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. Two people were killed in a drone strike on an Aramco oil field and one person died in an attack on an airport. The US has ordered non-emergency personnel and their families to leave the country. Today's guests: Francisco Blanch, Bank of America, Head of Global Commodities & Derivatives Research; Christian Keller, Barclays, Head of Economic Research. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Musk Calls for SpaceX-Tesla Mega Merger
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Berlin, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, global stocks gained as strong tech earnings eased concerns over the AI trade. SpaceX reported blowout third-quarter results with net income of $4.4 billion soaring past the average estimate of $1.88 billion. CEO Elon Musk seized on the momentum to call for a mega-merger with Tesla. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is due to speak at the company's GTC developer conference in Berlin. Today's guests: Lars-Hendrik Röller, Berlin Global Dialogue, Founder; Maria Ferraro, Siemens Energy, CFO; Martin Blessing, German Chancellor's Special Representative for Investments in Germany; Christian Sewing, Deutsche Bank, CEO. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: CME's Terry Duffy on the Disconcerting State of Finance Regulation
item.description:
The CFTC was practically brand new when Terry Duffy started working at the CME almost five decades ago, and over the course of his career at the exchange, this legend of the trading world has seen an enormous amount of change when it comes to finance regulation, including the rise of prediction markets, 24/7 trading and perpetual futures. Duffy is set to transition out of his current position as CME CEO next year, and this conversation, recorded live at City Winery in Chicago, is a sort of exit interview. He tells us how regulation has evolved since the start of his time at the CME. We also talk about why he is against perps, the credibility issues prediction markets face, his definition of spreads versus futures, and what he wishes he knew at the start of his career now that he is nearing retirement. (Source: Bloomberg)

On today's show, AI jitters returned after the Korean data center firm Elice flopped on its stock market debut. Shares fell as much as 35% after its IPO, which raised $151 million. Bloomberg has learnt that the AI cloud computing firm Nscale is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic, in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion. item.title: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
item.description:
History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The French Political Crisis Turning Into a Debt Crisis
item.description:
Just about everyone is worried about what is going on in France right now: the country's public finances are in sorry shape and there are fears that the French bond selloff, and the country's growing debt crisis, might spillover into the rest of Europe. The 2027 elections have investors worried: Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon aren't seen to be up to the task of taming France's fiscal turmoil. Shahin Vallée was an advisor to Emmanuel Macron when he was an economic minister and during his first presidential election campaign. He is currently a senior fellow at the German Council of Foreign Relations and advises institutional investors — and he understands what went wrong during Macron's nine years in office. Today, he speaks to us about the origins of the current French debt crisis, how similar it is to the challenges Greece faced during the first euro crisis, and why the 2027 elections are making an unstable situation even worse. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: Jeff Yan's Plan to Bring the Entire Financial Industry Onto Hyperliquid
item.description:
Traders and market watchers around the world started talking about a crypto platform called Hyperliquid earlier this year, when speculators used markets built on top of it to trade crude oil after war broke out in Iran. What Hyperliquid allowed for was a 24/7 market on the blockchain. In August, President Trump said the CFTC was working on bringing “Hyperliquid into the United States in a fully compliant and legal fashion.” Hyperliquid currently operates outside the US, but that hasn't stopped it from growing prodigiously in the last year. Jeff Yan, CEO and co-founder of Hyperliquid Labs, joins us today to explain how exactly the platform works, the protocol he and his co-founders built, the ecology of actors and assets that are tied to Hyperliquid (like the platform's cryptocurrency HYPE), how perps are bought and sold on the platform, what a blockchain oracle is, and what has to happen for Hyperliquid to start operating in the US. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Fed Weighs More Hikes on Inflation Concerns
item.description:

While rising Treasury yields and the bond selloff have added restraint, she said it is unclear whether conditions are restrictive enough. With oil prices rising again, further pressure on housing and auto demand could create uneven economic damage without resolving inflation. Sriram said the Fed’s approach, reflected in September meeting minutes, is focused on managing the risk that strong demand, persistent inflation or adverse supply shocks push prices higher. The Fed appears prepared to raise rates further, though she said a hike as soon as October is unlikely. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: MAIA: Interview of Guillaume Princen on Anthropic’s AI Strategy
item.description:
In an interview on October 14, 2026, Anthropic’s Head of International Startups & Digital Native, Guillaume Princen, discussed how startups and major firms are adopting Anthropic’s AI, including Claude tools, to boost employee productivity, overhaul processes, and build new products. He highlighted growing demand for frontier models like Opus 5.5, now about 40% cheaper than its predecessor, and a shift toward using different models for specific tasks across the 5.5 family. Princen emphasized Anthropic’s safety-first approach versus open-source and open-weight competitors, underscoring third-party auditing, closer cooperation with governments, and willingness to delay or limit powerful model releases—such as with Methos—if safety concerns arise, even at the expense of near-term revenue. Original filename: 20261014_080546_Interview_of_Guillaume_Princen_on_Anthropic_s_AI_Strategy.mp4 (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Brody Ford

item.title: Saudis Say New Missiles Intercepted After Deadly Airport Attacks
item.description:
US stock futures rose modestly as traders weighed the prospect of solid results in a busy week for corporate earnings against the risk of escalating tensions in the Middle East. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the kingdom overnight, including areas that are home to some of Saudi Arabia’s key oil and gas facilities. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest strikes since the Iran war began as Houthi militants repeatedly targeted airports across the kingdom, killing at least 14 people and wounding hundreds. The Opening Trade has everything you need to know as markets open across Europe. With analysis you won't find anywhere else, we break down the biggest stories of the day and speak to top guests who have skin in the game. Hosted by Anna Edwards, Guy Johnson and Tom Mackenzie. (Source: Bloomberg)
